DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93, Module 1.

Terminal objective

1.0 Given an engineering print, READ and INTERPRET the information contained in the title block, the notes and legend, the revision block, and the drawing grid. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.v

Enabling objectives

1.1 STATE the five types of information provided in the title block of an engineering drawing. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.v

1.2 STATE how the grid system on an engineering drawing is used to locate a piece of equipment. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.v

1.3 STATE the three types of information provided in the revision block of an engineering drawing. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.v

1.4 STATE the purpose of the notes and legend section of an engineering drawing. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.v

1.5 LIST the five drawing categories used on engineering drawings. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.v

Why the non-drawing areas matter

Objectives 1.1

"Engineering drawings are the industry's means of communicating detailed and accurate information on how to fabricate, assemble, troubleshoot, repair, and operate a piece of equipment or a system." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.1
"In this handbook the terms print, drawing, and diagram are used interchangeably to denote the complete drawing." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.1
  • Title block
  • Grid system
  • Revision block
  • Notes and legends
  • Engineering drawing (graphic portion)

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.2

The first four parts give important information about the actual drawing, and understanding them is as important as reading the drawing itself. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.2

"Failure to understand these areas can result in improper use or the misinterpretation of the drawing." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.2
"Because of the extreme variation in format, location of information, and types of information presented on drawings from vendor to vendor and site to site, all drawings will not necessarily contain the following information or format, but will usually be similar in nature." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.1

The title block

Objectives 1.1

"The title block of a drawing, usually located on the bottom or lower right hand corner, contains all the information necessary to identify the drawing and to verify its validity." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.2
"The first area of the title block contains the drawing title, the drawing number, and lists the location, the site, or the vendor." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.2

The drawing title and number are used for identification and filing. The number is usually unique to the drawing and is a code that can hold information such as the site, system, type of drawing, sheet number, or revision level. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.2

"Drawings are usually filed by their drawing number because the drawing title may be common to several prints or series of prints." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.2
"The second area of the title block contains the signatures and approval dates, which provide information as to when and by whom the component/system was designed and when and by whom the drawing was drafted and verified for final approval." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.2

These names can help locate further design or operating data, and can help resolve a discrepancy between the drawing and another source of information. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.2

"The third area of the title block is the reference block." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.3
"The reference block lists other drawings that are related to the system/component, or it can list all the other drawings that are cross-referenced on the drawing, depending on the site's or vendor's conventions." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.3

Other information, such as contract numbers and drawing scale, may also be in the title block and varies from site to site and vendor to vendor. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.3

  • The drawing title
  • The drawing number
  • Location, site, or vendor issuing the drawing
  • The design, review, and approval signatures
  • The reference block

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.9

Knowledge check: The title block

Objective 1.1Q1183

Why are drawings usually filed by drawing number instead of by title?

The answer is D. Drawings are usually filed by their drawing number because the drawing title may be common to several prints or series of prints. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.2

Report a problem
Objective 1.1Q1184

Which area of the title block lists other drawings related to the system or component?

The answer is A. The third area of the title block is the reference block, which lists related or cross-referenced drawings. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.3

Report a problem
Objective 1.1Q1185

Where is the title block usually located on a drawing?

The answer is C. The title block is usually located on the bottom or lower right hand corner. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.2

Drawing scale

Objectives 1.1

All drawings are either drawn to scale or not drawn to scale. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.4

"Drawings without a scale usually are intended to present only functional information about the component or system." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.4
"Scale drawings usually present the information used to fabricate or construct a component or system." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.4

Not every dimension has to be written on a scale drawing, because the user can measure the distance on the drawing and divide or multiply by the stated scale. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.4

  • 1" = 1" is read as 1 inch on the drawing equals 1 inch on the component. It can also be stated as FULL SIZE.
  • 3/8" = 1' is read as 3/8 inch on the drawing equals 1 foot on the component.
  • 1/2" = 1' is read as 1/2 inch on the drawing equals 1 foot on the component.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.4

Knowledge check: Drawing scale

Objective 1.1Q1186

A drawing scale reads 3/8" = 1'. A part measures 9/8 inch on the drawing. How long is the actual part?

The answer is C. 9/8 inch divided by 3/8 inch per foot is 3 feet. The handbook example uses 6/8 inch for 2 feet. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.4

Objective 1.1Q1187

What do drawings without a scale usually present?

The answer is A. Drawings without a scale usually are intended to present only functional information about the component or system. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.4

The grid system

Objectives 1.2

Drawings tend to be large and complex, so finding a specific point can be difficult, especially when a wire or pipe run continues on a second drawing. Most drawings, especially P&IDs and electrical schematics, have a grid system. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.5

"The grid can consist of letters, numbers, or both that run horizontally and vertically around the drawing as illustrated on Figure 2." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.5
"Like a city map, the drawing is divided into smaller blocks, each having a unique two letter or number identifier." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.5
"For example, when a pipe is continued from one drawing to another, not only is the second drawing referenced on the first drawing, but so are the grid coordinates locating the continued pipe." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.5

Searching the one block is much easier than searching the whole drawing. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.5

When a pipe continues from one drawing to another, what does the first drawing reference?

The answer is C. Like a city map, the drawing is divided into smaller blocks, each having a unique two letter or number identifier. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.5

The revision block

Objectives 1.3

When a component or system changes, the drawings that show it must be redrafted and reissued. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.6

"When a drawing is first issued, it is called revision zero, and the revision block is empty." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.6

An entry is placed in the revision block as each revision is made. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.6

"This entry will provide the revision number, a title or summary of the revision, and the date of the revision." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.6

The revision number may also appear at the end of the drawing number or in its own block. It goes up by one with each update, and the drawing number stays the same. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.6

"The old Revision 2 drawing will be filed and maintained in the filing system for historical purposes." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.6

There are two common ways to show where a revision changed a drawing: a hand-drawn cloud around each change, or a circle, triangle, or other shape holding the revision number next to each affected portion. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.7

"The cloud method indicates changes from the most recent revision only, whereas the second method indicates all revisions to the drawing because all of the previous revision circles remain on the drawing." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.7

Which part of a drawing gives the revision number, a summary of the revision, and its date?

What is a drawing called when it is first issued?

The answer is A. When a drawing is first issued, it is called revision zero, and the revision block is empty. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.6

Objective 1.3Q1191

Which method of marking changes shows only the most recent revision?

The answer is B. The cloud method indicates changes from the most recent revision only. Revision circles stay on the drawing and show all revisions. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.7

Notes and legend

Objectives 1.4

Most symbols and lines are self-explanatory or standard, but a few unique symbols and conventions must be explained for each drawing. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.8

"The notes and legends section of a drawing lists and explains any special symbols and conventions used on the drawing, as illustrated on Figure 5." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.8

The notes section also lists any information the designer or draftsman felt was necessary to use or understand the drawing correctly. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.8

"Because of the importance of understanding all of the symbols and conventions used on a drawing, the notes and legend section must be reviewed before reading a drawing." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.8

The five drawing categories

Objectives 1.5

"They are 1) piping and instrument drawings (P&IDs), 2) electrical single lines and schematics, 3) electronic diagrams and schematics, 4) logic diagrams and prints, and 5) fabrication, construction, and architectural drawings." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.10
"As a rule P&IDs do not have a drawing scale and present only the relationship or sequence between components." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.11

Two pieces of equipment drawn side by side are not necessarily even in the same building. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.11

"These drawings only present information on how a system functions, not the actual physical relationships." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.11

Electrical single lines and schematics give the same kind of functional information for electrical systems that P&IDs give for piping and instrument systems, and are usually not drawn to scale. Schematics give more detail than single lines, such as individual relays, relay contacts, fuses, motors, lights, and instrument sensors. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.11

"Electronic diagrams and schematics are designed to present information about the individual components (resistors, transistors, and capacitors) used in a circuit, as illustrated in Figure 9." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.13

These drawings are usually used by circuit designers and electronics repair personnel. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.13

"The most common use is to provide a simplified functional representation of an electrical circuit, as illustrated in Figure 10." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.14
"These drawings do not replace schematics, but they are easier to use for certain applications." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.14
"Fabrication, construction, and architectural drawings are designed to present the detailed information required to construct or fabricate a part, system, or structure." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.14

Construction drawings give the detail to assemble a structure on site. Architectural drawings give the conceptual design of a building or structure. Fabrication drawings are usually found in machine shops and give a craftsman the detail to fabricate a part. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.14

"All three types of drawings, fabrication, construction, and architectural, are usually drawn to scale." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.14

Two pumps are drawn next to each other on a P&ID. What does that tell you?

The answer is D. P&IDs present only the relationship or sequence between components, not the actual physical relationships. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.11

Report a problem
Objective 1.5Q1195

Do logic prints replace electrical schematics?

The answer is A. These drawings do not replace schematics, but they are easier to use for certain applications. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.14

Report a problem
Objective 1.5Q1196

Which drawing category is usually drawn to scale?

The answer is D. All three types of drawings, fabrication, construction, and architectural, are usually drawn to scale. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.14

Drawing formats

Objectives 1.0

"The standard formats are single line, pictorial or double line, and cutaway." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.16
"The single line format represents all piping, regardless of size, as single line." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.16

By simplifying piping and equipment, single lines let the reader clearly understand how the equipment and instruments relate. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.16

"Pictorial or double line drawings present the same type information as a single line, but the equipment is represented as if it had been photographed." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.16

This format is rarely used because it takes more effort than a single line and adds no information on how the system functions. It is often used in advertising and training material. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.16

"As seen in Figure 14, an assembly drawing is a pictorial view of the object with all the components shown as they go together." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.17

Assembly drawings are usually found in vendor manuals and are used for parts identification and general assembly information. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.17

"In a cutaway, as the name implies, the component or system has a portion cut away to reveal the internal parts of the component or system." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.18

Cutaways are very helpful in maintenance and training, where the way internal parts are assembled matters. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.18

Views and perspectives

Objectives 1.0

Formats can be drawn in different views. The most common are the orthographic projection and the isometric projection. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.19

"Orthographic projections present the component or system through the use of three views," DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.19
  • A top view
  • A side view
  • A front view

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.19

Other views, such as a bottom view, are used when needed. Orthographic projection is widely used for fabrication and construction drawings. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.19

The three views, with dimensions and a drawing scale, contain the information needed to fabricate or construct the component or system. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.20

"The isometric projection presents a single view of the component or system." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.21
"The view is commonly from above and at an angle of 30°." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.21

This view makes it easier to see how the system looks and how its parts relate to one another. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.21

"Isometric projections may or may not be drawn to a scale." DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.21

Worked examples

Objective 1.1

Reading a drawing scale

A drawing scale reads 3/8" = 1'. A component part measures 6/8 inch on the drawing. How long is the actual part?

  1. Read the scale: 3/8 inch on the drawing equals 1 foot on the component.
  2. Divide the measured length by the scale: 6/8 divided by 3/8 is 2.

Answer: The actual component measures 2 feet.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.4

Objective 1.1

Reading a second scale

A drawing scale reads 1/2" = 1'. A part measures 1-1/2 inches on the drawing. How long is the actual part?

  1. Read the scale: 1/2 inch on the drawing equals 1 foot on the component.
  2. Divide the measured length by the scale: 1-1/2 divided by 1/2 is 3.

Answer: The actual component measures 3 feet.

DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.4

Summary

  • The title block of a drawing contains the drawing title, the drawing number, the location, site, or vendor, the design, review, and approval signatures, and the reference block. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.9
  • The grid system allows information to be more easily identified, using coordinate letters and numbers that break the drawing into smaller blocks. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.9
  • The revision block provides the revision number, a title or summary, and the date of each revision. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.9
  • The notes and legend section explains special symbols or conventions, and any other information needed to understand the drawing. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.9
  • The five drawing categories are P&IDs, electrical single lines and schematics, electronic diagrams and schematics, logic diagrams and prints, and fabrication, construction, and architectural drawings. DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93 PR-01 p.22
